title: Perspectives on science and art
authors: Bevil R. Conway; Margaret S. Livingstone
key_findings: Fixations concentrate on regions of high local contrast (citing Reinagel & Zador 1999); eyes attract gaze partly because they hold high local contrast.
Shadows must be locally darker and relatively desaturated to read as shadows (citing Kingdom et al. 2004/2005); their hue can be almost anything.
Faces stay recognisable at low resolution and in simplified/exaggerated forms (citing Sinha et al. 2006); simplified stencil shapes remain recognisable.
Artists were more often strabismic than non-artists in the authors' survey; reduced stereo may favour monocular cues (shading, occlusion, perspective).
Depth from shading need not be globally consistent; viewers accept physically impossible shadows/reflections (citing Cavanagh 2005).
practical_applications: Put the strongest local contrast where the eye should land (focal glasses, a character's head).
Stylised charcoal shadows only need to be darker (and greyer) than their surroundings; their exact geometry is free.
limitations: Short review; value structure (notan) itself is not discussed.
Strabismus link is correlational.

title: Building the gist of a scene: the role of global image features in recognition
key_findings: Scene gist can be computed from a low-dimensional global code of spatial layout (spatial envelope) without first recognising objects.
With brief presentations observers rely on the low-spatial-frequency part of hybrid images; longer viewing shifts reliance to finer content.
Processing runs global-to-local, which does not have to mean a fixed low-to-high spatial-frequency order.
practical_applications: The coarse, blurred, small version of an image (its big value masses) is what a scrolling viewer gets first: design and test it.
Thumbnail/blur checks are a proxy for first-glance reading.
limitations: Read via abstract and preprint excerpts, not full text.
Natural scenes, not illustrations or layouts.

title: From blobs to boundary edges: Evidence for time- and spatial-scale-dependent scene recognition
key_findings: A coarse description (oriented 'blobs' in a spatial arrangement) can initiate scene recognition before object identity is processed.
At ~30 ms masked presentation observers used the low-spatial-frequency part of hybrid images; at longer durations the high-frequency part (as summarised by Oliva & Torralba).
practical_applications: Big value blobs carry the first read; fine line/texture is read later.
A blurred/thumbnail check approximates the first tens of ms of viewing.
limitations: Accuracy figures not seen; summary via abstract and secondary review.

title: The briefest of glances: The time course of natural scene understanding
key_findings: 75%-correct thresholds with masking: global properties (naturalness, openness, depth...) mean 34 ms (19-47 ms); basic-level categories mean 50 ms (30-67 ms).
Global layout properties are available before the scene is named; 20 participants, 548 landscape photos at 256x256 px.
practical_applications: The overall structure of an image (open/closed, deep/flat, light/dark) is read within tens of ms: set it with value masses before detail.
Supports testing images at small size: what survives 256 px and a glance is the design.
limitations: Landscape photographs only; masked lab presentation differs from feed scrolling.

title: How many pixels make an image?
key_findings: Human scene categorisation stays high across low-resolution and multi-megapixel images.
(Secondary summary) Viewers classify scenes and identify several objects at 32x32 pixels.
practical_applications: A 32x32 colour or 64-px greyscale thumbnail is a defensible 'gist' test size: subject and scene type should still read.
limitations: Exact accuracy per resolution not read (full text not accessed).

title: Is it warm? Is it real? Or just low spatial frequency?
key_findings: (Secondary summaries) The Mona Lisa's smile is carried mainly by low spatial frequencies, so it is more visible in peripheral vision and fades when looked at directly.
Later work (Kontsevich & Tyler 2004) tested the claim with noise manipulations.
practical_applications: Soft, low-frequency value shapes can carry mood that survives a glance and the periphery; crisp detail is only seen where the viewer looks.
limitations: Original letter not read; content from press and citing papers.

title: Rembrandt's textural agency: A shared perspective in visual art and science
authors: Steve DiPaola; Caitlin Riebe; James T. Enns
key_findings: Rembrandt varied detail selectively ('textural agency') to guide gaze; with Rembrandt-style renderings of photographed portraits, viewers fixated the detailed eye faster and longer, with calmer eye movements.
Viewers preferred the selectively detailed renderings to the uniformly detailed original photographs (press summary).
practical_applications: Keep the sharpest, finest detail on the focal feature (glasses, a hand, part of a face) and reduce it elsewhere.
Calmer viewing paths come from a single detail peak, not uniform sharpness.
limitations: Abstract and press summaries only; numeric results not read.
Portraits only.

title: Following the masters: Portrait viewing and appreciation is guided by selective detail
authors: Steve DiPaola; Caitlin Riebe; James T. Enns
key_findings: (Abstract excerpt/summaries) Painted portraits differ from photos in that selected regions are rendered in sharper detail; gaze was attracted to and held longer by regions of finer detail and by textural highlighting.
The study set out to separate detail from confounds (meaning, lighting) that usually co-occur with detail.
practical_applications: Detail is a lever separate from value contrast: it can place the eye even when lighting is even.
limitations: Full abstract and results not read; Perception 42(6):608-630 per library record.

title: Measuring visual clutter
authors: Ruth Rosenholtz; Yuanzhen Li; Lisa Nakano
key_findings: Proposes Feature Congestion, Subband Entropy and Edge Density as image-computable clutter measures; clutter = how hard it is to add an item that captures attention.
Colour variability matters for clutter (captured only by Feature Congestion).
A later review reports simple edge density predicting search difficulty about as well as feature congestion.
practical_applications: Edge density (edge pixels / area) is a cheap, evidence-linked clutter proxy for backgrounds behind text or the hero.
limitations: Abstract and repository page only; validated on maps/scenes, not illustrations.

title: Capabilities and limitations of peripheral vision
key_findings: Peripheral vision supports many tasks despite losing much information; a lossy, relatively fixed peripheral encoding may explain the difficulty of peripheral recognition, search, change blindness and gist.
practical_applications: Outside the focal zone viewers get a summary of detail; spend detail where the eye lands and keep the periphery statistically calm.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: Visual crowding: a fundamental limit on conscious perception and object recognition
key_findings: Crowding - impaired identification of an object among nearby clutter - limits perception across much of the visual field.
(Secondary) The crowding zone is roughly half the target's eccentricity (Bouma's rule).
practical_applications: Small details (logo, temple engraving, lettering) placed near other detail in the periphery will not be identified; give them space or move them to the focal zone.
limitations: Abstract and secondary statements; Bouma figure from citing reviews.

title: Isophote distance: a shading approach to artistic stroke thickness
authors: Todd Goodwin; Ian Vollick; Aaron Hertzmann
key_findings: Stroke thickness modelled as the image-space distance to the nearest isophote: thicker for nearer and less-curved forms, thinner for distant and highly curved ones; clamped to [Tmin, Tmax].
Reproduced the line weights of illustration examples with few parameters.
practical_applications: Rule set for line weight in pencil/charcoal and rig line art: weight by depth, form size, curvature and light side.
limitations: Graphics method validated by visual comparison, not perception experiments.
Spot-check 2026-11-25: original wording checked; finding corrected to match the source.

title: How to Draw Pictures, Part 4: Line Thickness
key_findings: Line thickness falls with distance and with radial curvature; thick forms get thicker strokes; strokes thicker on the underside of forms lit from above.
Silhouettes usually thicker than interior lines; strokes taper at free ends but not where they pass behind another object.
Artists compress the thickness range and care about relative differences; the author says these trends are observations, not systematic tests.
practical_applications: Direct line-weight checklist for Mint & Tao pencil art and SVG rig strokes.
limitations: Expert blog by a graphics researcher; observations, not experiments.

title: Why do line drawings work? A realism hypothesis
key_findings: Hypothesis: the visual system treats line drawings as approximately realistic renderings; drawing techniques are chosen to convey shape to a human observer.
Argues an edge-detector account (Sayim & Cavanagh 2011) cannot fully explain differences between photo edges and drawn lines.
practical_applications: Draw the lines a plausible shading of the form would produce (contours, creases), not every edge in a reference photo.
limitations: Theoretical paper; abstract and introduction only.

title: What line drawings reveal about the visual brain
key_findings: Lines in standard drawings stand for depth or slant discontinuities; artists omit shadow borders, which would read as false object boundaries.
Line drawings are recognised by infants, people without pictorial culture and chimpanzees - not purely a learned convention.
Junctions carry 3D meaning: T = occlusion, Y = convex corner, X = transparency; contours may end where a smooth surface turns away.
practical_applications: Pencil/charcoal line art: draw occluding contours and creases, end lines where forms turn, keep clean T-junctions at overlaps; use X-junctions (background line continuing through the lens) for glass.
limitations: Perspective article; synthesis, not new experiments.

title: Where do people draw lines?
authors: Forrester Cole; Aleksey Golovinskiy; Alex Limpaecher; Heather Stoddart Barros; Adam Finkelstein; Thomas Funkhouser; Szymon Rusinkiewicz
key_findings: Artists' lines for the same 3D shape largely overlap (75% within 1 mm of another artist's line), especially along occluding contours.
Most non-contour lines lie on large image-intensity gradients and match line-drawing algorithms; 14% were not explained by any local property studied.
practical_applications: Occluding contours are the non-negotiable lines; interior lines go where shading changes fast. Use this to judge AI 'line art' that adds random interior lines.
limitations: Abstract/project page; small artist sample; smooth 3D models, not characters.

title: Stylization and abstraction of photographs
key_findings: Stylises photographs into line-and-region abstractions, keeping detail where viewers' eye movements show meaningful content and removing it elsewhere.
practical_applications: Model for selective detail: keep structure and detail at fixated/meaningful regions, flatten the rest into large regions.
limitations: Abstract and course summary; evaluation details not read.

title: Abstracted painterly renderings using eye-tracking data
key_findings: Uses a few seconds of a viewer's eye-tracking data to decide where a painterly rendering keeps detail; elsewhere strokes are larger and simpler.
practical_applications: Detail allocation can follow where people look; our proxy is the saliency map from analyze_image.py.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: Simple line drawings suffice for functional MRI decoding of natural scene categories
authors: Dirk B. Walther; Barry Chai; Eamon Caddigan; Diane M. Beck; Li Fei-Fei
key_findings: Scene category decoded from fMRI activity for line drawings as well as for colour photographs, from V1 to PPA/RSC.
Global scene structure preserved by line drawings is integral to scene-category representation.
practical_applications: Line-art backgrounds for Mint & Tao can carry place (cafe, beach, street) with a few structural lines; texture everywhere is not needed.
limitations: Six scene categories; abstract and press release.

title: Photographic tone reproduction for digital images
authors: Erik Reinhard; Michael Stark; Peter Shirley; James Ferwerda
key_findings: Maps high-dynamic-range scene luminance to a low-range display using ideas from Ansel Adams' Zone System (11 print zones, 0 black to X white; key value; dodging-and-burning).
A simple global operator plus local dodging-and-burning gave good results across many test images (authors' report).
practical_applications: Tonal compression vocabulary: choose the key (where middle grey sits), roll off highlights instead of clipping, keep local contrast at the subject.
limitations: Abstract and summaries; graphics evaluation, not perceptual experiments.

title: Global nonlinear compression of natural luminances in painted art
authors: Daniel J. Graham; David J. Field
key_findings: Paintings cannot reproduce natural luminance ranges; a log-like nonlinearity is a first approximation of how artists compress luminance.
A painter's global compression curve ('artist's look-up table') may be characteristic of a painter; Western observers preferred many such transforms over a plain log transform.
practical_applications: Tonal compression is a style choice: define a 'house curve' per series (e.g. charcoal: lifted blacks, compressed mids) and keep it.
limitations: Conference proceedings; abstract and excerpts.

title: Application of Fourier analysis to the visibility of gratings
authors: F. W. Campbell; J. G. Robson
key_findings: Grating detection thresholds for different waveforms relate through Fourier theory; proposes independent mechanisms tuned to limited spatial-frequency ranges.
(Secondary) The contrast sensitivity function is band-pass, peaking around a few cycles per degree.
practical_applications: Very fine texture at phone viewing distance is near-invisible; mid-scale marks carry most visible contrast.
limitations: Peak value from secondary summary.

title: Does luminance-contrast contribute to a saliency map for overt visual attention?
key_findings: Contrast is elevated at fixated points, but when contrast was modified in natural images no causal contribution of luminance contrast to overt attention was detected; saliency may be computed late.
Parkhurst & Niebur (2004) re-explained the data with second-order (texture) contrast.
practical_applications: Contested note: raw value contrast alone does not guarantee gaze; combine it with detail, meaning (faces, product) and isolation.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: Visual correlates of fixation selection: effects of scale and time
authors: Benjamin W. Tatler; Roland J. Baddeley; Iain D. Gilchrist
key_findings: Image features at fixation contributed similarly across viewing time (unlike Parkhurst et al. 2002).
(Secondary) Edge content and contrast were stronger fixation predictors than colour in these authors' work.
practical_applications: Edges are a stronger gaze lever than hue alone: keep the hardest edges at the focal area.
limitations: Search summary and secondary descriptions only.

title: Colour vision brings clarity to shadows
authors: Frederick A. A. Kingdom; Catherine Beauce; Lyndsay Hunter
key_findings: Colour vision helps identify shadows among other luminance changes; shadows carry shape, depth and movement information once identified.
practical_applications: Shadow masses read best when darker AND slightly desaturated relative to the lit surface; coloured shadows are fine if this holds.
limitations: Abstract and later citations.

title: Prior knowledge on the illumination position
key_findings: Shape-from-shading assumes light from above, biased toward above-left (about 20-30 degrees per a companion paper); one later study found no left bias.
practical_applications: Light flat line-art and charcoal forms from upper-left by default so bumps read as bumps; reverse only on purpose.
limitations: Abstract/secondary; left bias is contested.

title: Face recognition by humans: Nineteen results all computer vision researchers should know about
authors: Pawan Sinha; Benjamin Balas; Yuri Ostrovsky; Richard Russell
key_findings: Familiar faces are recognised at very low resolution (high accuracy at 16x16 blocks in a cited study).
practical_applications: Identity is carried by coarse configuration; for faceless Mint & Tao the coarse silhouette (hair mass, head shape, posture) must carry identity instead.
limitations: Search summary; the caricature result attributed to this paper by Conway & Livingstone was not seen directly.

title: Identification of everyday objects on the basis of silhouette and outline versions
key_findings: Identification of filled silhouettes and outlines of Snodgrass-Vanderwart objects ranged from near zero to perfect depending on the object; norms widely reused.
practical_applications: Silhouette readability is object- and view-dependent: choose the view (pose, angle of the glasses) whose silhouette identifies it, and test it.
limitations: Abstract; full author list not checked.

title: Humans prefer curved visual objects
key_findings: Objects with curved contours were liked more than sharp-angled versions, for real objects and meaningless patterns; authors proposed sharp angles signal threat.
practical_applications: Rounded shapes as the default for friendly characters/mascots and calm promo layouts.
limitations: Abstract; threat explanation later contested (Bertamini 2016).

title: Do people prefer curved objects? Angularity, expertise, and aesthetic preference
authors: Paul J. Silvia; Christopher M. Barona
key_findings: (Via citing papers) Curvature preference held after controlling perceived complexity, using regular and irregular polygons; expertise effects were inconsistent across studies.
practical_applications: Curvature preference is not a reason to avoid angular design for expert audiences; test.
limitations: Paper not reached; content only from Bertamini 2016 and Cotter 2017 citations.

title: Do observers like curvature or do they dislike angularity?
authors: Marco Bertamini; Letizia Palumbo; Tamara N. Gheorghes; Mai Galatsidas
key_findings: Four experiments: curved shapes preferred (about 50 vs 37 on the rating scale), not explained by complexity; curved lines preferred to both straight and angular lines.
Approach to curves but no avoidance of angles in an implicit task; a threat account cannot fully explain the effect.
Cites Leder, Tinio & Bar (2011): curvature preference vanished for negatively valenced objects.
practical_applications: Use curves to add warmth; use angles for energy/tension rather than expecting 'danger' by default.
limitations: Small samples (14-36); some statistic reporting inconsistencies noted on reading.

title: Comparing angular and curved shapes in terms of implicit associations and approach/avoidance responses
authors: Letizia Palumbo; Nicole Ruta; Marco Bertamini
key_findings: IAT: curved polygons associated with positive and safe (and a gender pattern), angular with negative and danger.
A manikin approach/avoidance task did not show the pattern a pure threat account predicts.
practical_applications: Round = positive/safe and angular = negative/danger are measurable implicit associations at the abstract-shape level.
limitations: Abstract; abstract polygons, not characters.

title: How universal is preference for visual curvature? A systematic review and meta-analysis
key_findings: 61 studies, 106 samples, 309 effects, about 11,000 participants: curvature preference g = 0.39 [0.25, 0.52].
Larger with limited presentation time (g 0.75 vs 0.32), meaningless stimuli (0.56) and real objects (0.42); no effect for spatial designs (-0.04); experts small and n.s. (0.13).
Large heterogeneity; no clear small-study bias. Reliable but not universal.
practical_applications: At glance speed (feeds) curvature helps most; for experts and architecture-like layouts it matters little. A default lean, not a law.
limitations: Only continuous measures; culture not tested as a moderator; about two thirds of the full text read.

title: The bouba/kiki effect is robust across cultures and writing systems
authors: Aleksandra Ćwiek et al. (incl. Marcus Perlman)
key_findings: 917 speakers of 25 languages (9 families, 10 writing systems): strong overall evidence for the bouba/kiki effect; bouba more consistent than kiki; largely independent of orthography.
practical_applications: Round shapes match soft-sounding names and voices; pair round mascots with soft names/voices, spiky ones with sharp.
limitations: Abstract and press; whether Thai was among the languages not confirmed.

title: Synaesthesia - A window into perception, thought and language
authors: V. S. Ramachandran; Edward M. Hubbard
key_findings: Named the bouba/kiki effect (after Köhler's takete/baluba) and argued that naming is not fully arbitrary.
practical_applications: Historical anchor for shape-sound mapping; use Cwiek2022 for robust evidence.
limitations: Not read; the widely quoted agreement percentage was not verified.

title: Universal aesthetic of fractals
authors: Branka Spehar; Colin W. G. Clifford; Ben R. Newell; Richard P. Taylor
key_findings: (Secondary) Preference for fractal patterns peaks at mid fractal dimension (about 1.3-1.5) across natural, mathematical and painted (Pollock) fractals.
Later work (Spehar et al. 2016; Street et al. 2016) reports individual differences and treats 'universal' cautiously.
practical_applications: Detail density: moderate complexity is liked more than sparse or dense; a texture field should not be maximally busy.
limitations: Paper not read; claims from citing reviews.

title: The glasses stereotype revisited: Effects of eyeglasses on perception, recognition, and impression of faces
authors: Helmut Leder; Michael Forster; Gernot Gerger
key_findings: Faces with full-rim glasses rated less attractive and likeable than without; rimless did not differ; both rated more intelligent and successful; rimless raised trustworthiness.
Glasses drew gaze to the eye region; rimless made faces less distinctive.
practical_applications: Frame visibility changes impressions: full-rim adds intelligence/competence cues; rimless keeps the face's own look. Nothing here on face-shape matching.
limitations: Abstract; European sample.

title: The effect of the shape of eyeglasses on judgements of personality
key_findings: 39 Japanese undergraduates imagined wearing round or square eyeglasses: round -> rated self warmer; square -> more competent and more stubborn.
Face shape was not manipulated; small between-subjects sample; main ANOVA statistics not reported in the text.
practical_applications: Weak, preliminary support that round frames read warm and square frames read competent; face-shape matching advice remains retail convention.
limitations: Very small N; conference proceedings; self-ratings of imagined wear.

title: Is artists' perception more veridical?
key_findings: Artists were as affected by visual context and constancies (size, lightness, shape) as novices; no special access to the retinal image.
Later work (2014) links drawing skill to efficient encoding of object structure; Ostrofsky et al. report a constancy-accuracy correlation (mixed evidence).
practical_applications: Value judged by eye on a colour image is unreliable even for trained artists: check value in greyscale/numerically.
limitations: Search summary of abstracts.

title: Munsell Value (How Color Notation Works)
key_findings: Munsell value runs 0 (black) to 10 (white) in perceptually equal steps; N5 is middle grey; real pigments only approach N0/N10.
practical_applications: Use the 0-10 value vocabulary in briefs; a 5-value plan maps roughly to N2, N4, N5-6, N7-8, N9.
limitations: Search summary of the page.

title: ISO/CIE 11664-4:2019 Colorimetry - Part 4: CIE 1976 L*a*b* colour space
key_findings: Specifies CIELAB coordinates including the lightness correlate L* (cube root of relative luminance with a linear segment near black; 0-100).
practical_applications: Numeric value thresholds can be stated in L*; for neutrals OKLab L = (L*+16)/116 above the dark linear segment.
limitations: Standard text not read; formula as quoted in secondary encyclopedic sources.

title: Plein-air tip: grouping tonal values
key_findings: Organising values into a light group and a dark group is 'an essential composition strategy'; connect darks into one unbroken mass instead of scattered accents; reserve high contrast for what should be noticed.
A simple tonal design reads at a glance and at small size (reply in comments); 'shape welding' merges adjacent similar values.
practical_applications: Mass shadows of figure and furniture into one dark shape in charcoal stories; keep the light group simple.
limitations: Practitioner blog; no tests.

title: Edges (lesson series) and Designing Value Groups (course)
key_findings: (Search summaries) Start from hard edges, then soften transitions and lose edges in shadow to steer the eye to the focal point; squinting groups values and blurs detail.
practical_applications: Edge pass procedure for painted/FLUX images: decide the hard edges first, lose the rest.
limitations: Only search snippets read.

title: Creating Characters with Personality: For Film, TV, Animation, Video Games, and Graphic Novels
key_findings: (Via student papers) Proportion and body shape create visual interest and reveal personality; a widely cited source for shape-language character design.
practical_applications: Practitioner basis for primary/secondary shape design of mascots and Mint & Tao silhouettes.
limitations: Not read; publisher and year not confirmed this session.
